title: Saint Thérèse of the Child Jesus, Virgin and Doctor of the Church
short_summary: Saint Thérèse of Lisieux (1873-1897) was a French Discalced Carmelite whose short life in an enclosed monastery became influential through her autobiographical writings. Her teaching on spiritual childhood and trust in God's mercy, often called the little way, led John Paul II to declare her a Doctor of the Church.
key_facts: The U.S. calendar keeps Saint Thérèse as a memorial on October 1.
She entered the Carmel of Lisieux in 1888 at the age of fifteen.
Her autobiographical manuscripts were published after her death as Story of a Soul.
She was canonized in 1925, named a principal patron of Catholic missions in 1927, and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1997.

sections.heading: Family and early life
sections.body: Marie-Françoise-Thérèse Martin was born at Alençon in Normandy on January 2, 1873, the youngest surviving child of Louis and Zélie Martin. Her mother's death in 1877 deeply affected her, and the family moved to Lisieux. Her four surviving sisters eventually entered religious life. Thérèse described a decisive interior change at Christmas 1886 that freed her from an intense childhood sensitivity and clarified her vocation.

sections.heading: Carmel of Lisieux
sections.body: Thérèse sought admission to Carmel before the customary age and personally appealed to Pope Leo XIII during a pilgrimage to Rome. She entered in April 1888, received the name Thérèse of the Child Jesus and of the Holy Face, and made profession in 1890. Her life consisted of the ordinary prayer, work, relationships, and hidden sacrifices of an enclosed Carmelite community. She also wrote poems, plays, prayers, and letters, including correspondence with missionary priests.

sections.heading: The little way
sections.body: Thérèse recognized that she could not reach holiness through impressive achievements. She instead placed complete confidence in the mercy of God and sought to perform small actions with love. Her spiritual childhood was neither passivity nor sentimentality; it joined awareness of personal weakness to confidence in the Father and an exacting practice of charity toward the sisters with whom she lived.

sections.heading: Illness, writings, and recognition
sections.body: Tuberculosis brought severe physical suffering, while her final months also included a trial of faith that she described as darkness. She died on September 30, 1897, at twenty-four. Manuscripts written at the request of her superiors were edited and published as Story of a Soul, spreading her teaching worldwide. Pius XI canonized her in 1925. John Paul II declared her a Doctor of the Church in 1997 for the depth and lasting influence of her spiritual doctrine.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Spiritual childhood
catholic_connection_sections.body: Thérèse's little way depends on grace. It approaches God with the trust of a child while accepting the concrete demands of love, repentance, perseverance, and self-gift.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Patron of missions
catholic_connection_sections.body: Although she never left her monastery after entering Carmel, Thérèse offered prayer and suffering for the Church's missionaries and corresponded with missionary priests. Her patronage expresses the Catholic belief that contemplation and apostolic work belong to one mission.

historical_cautions: Story of a Soul was assembled from several manuscripts and was edited in early editions; later critical editions distinguish Thérèse's original texts.
Avoid reducing the little way to cheerfulness or easy devotion; her writings include ascetic discipline, psychological suffering, and a severe final trial of faith.
